posts.caption:
Depreciation goes up by 10. Walk me through the three statements.

That's the real question. Anyone can name the three. What separates people is taking one line, changing it, and tracing it through all of them without stopping.

Net income falls 7.5, not 10, because the tax saving is real cash you keep.
Add the depreciation back and cash is up 2.5.
Assets fall 7.5, equity falls 7.5, and it balances.

Say "and it balances" out loud at the end. That's the sentence the interviewer is waiting for, and most people stop one line short of it.

State your tax rate before you start. 25% is fine. Picking one and saying it is part of the answer.

Save this for the night before.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #financialmodeling #accountinginterview

"Tell me about yourself" is the only question you know is coming. Most people still waste it.

90 seconds. 3 beats. One thread running through all of them.

Beat 1, where you started. 20 seconds, not 60. Where you're from, what you study, enough to place you. Then move.

Beat 2 is the only part they'll remember. One decision and what you did about it. A deal you followed, a club you joined, a model you built at 2am because you wanted to know how it worked. This is where a person shows up instead of a candidate.

Beat 3 points at the door. "Which is why I want to be in this seat, at this bank." It hands them the follow-up question you actually want.

Then cut it. A written answer of 220 words is about 90 seconds spoken. Most people deliver over 3 minutes and don't notice, because rehearsing in your head is always faster than saying it out loud.

Time it with a stopwatch. Once.

Save this.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #interviewprep #financecareers

Terminal value is 60 to 80% of your DCF. Most people spend 90% of their prep on the other 20%.

6 steps, in order. Project unlevered free cash flow for 5 years. Pick a WACC. Discount. Build terminal value. Discount that too. Bridge to equity.

Step 4 is where people fall apart.

Gordon growth takes your year 5 cash flow, grows it at g, and divides by WACC minus g. Keep g under long-run GDP growth, call it 2 to 3%. Quote 5% and you've just claimed the company eventually becomes the entire economy.

Two more things they're listening for.

Unlevered cash flow pairs with WACC. It's before interest, so it belongs to lenders and shareholders together. Pair it with cost of equity instead and you've counted the capital structure twice.

And a DCF gives you enterprise value, not a share price. Subtract net debt. Subtract preferred and minority interest. Divide by diluted shares. They asked for the share price.

Last thing. Don't call it the most accurate method. It's the most assumption-heavy one, and saying so is what makes you sound like you've built one rather than read about one.

Save this before your next technical.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #dcf #valuation

5 questions. Answer all five cold and you're ahead of most people in an investment banking first round.

The 3 statements. Enterprise value versus equity value. The DCF. Accretion and dilution. How a profitable company runs out of cash.

Every investment banking interview pulls from the same small set of technical questions. The names change, the order changes, the questions don't.

Each one here comes with the answer, and with the mistake that costs people the offer.

Two new technical questions every day, starting now.

Save this one for the night before.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #financecareers #valuation

posts.caption:
A comp set isn't a list. It's an argument that the market should value your target exactly the way it values these 8 companies, so every name you include is a claim you have to be ready to defend out loud.

Screen on the business, not the label. Same model, similar size and growth, same geography, same customer. 2 companies can share an industry code and have nothing in common economically.

A sector screen isn't a comp set. It's 40 tickers.

Then pick the multiple the capital structure allows. EV/EBITDA ignores use, so it compares companies financed completely differently. P/E sits after interest, so debt contaminates it, and you should use it only where use genuinely matches.

Calendarise. A December filer and a June filer are 6 months apart.

Nobody mentions it until a VP does.

Use the median, never the mean. 1 outlier drags an average in a set of 8, so show the quartile range too and let the reader see how tight it actually is.

And explain your outliers rather than deleting them. The name trading at twice the median is the most interesting thing in the set.

Save this one.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #comparablecompanies

Your whole DCF rests on 1 number, and most candidates can't defend it.

WACC. Every term, and where each one comes from.

The weights are market value, not book. Equity weight uses market cap. Pulling book equity off the balance sheet is the single most common slip here.

Cost of debt is after tax. 100 of interest at a 25% rate costs the company 75, because the deduction is real. There's no equivalent on equity, since dividends aren't deductible. Haircut both and you've misunderstood why the haircut exists at all.

Cost of equity comes from CAPM. Risk-free rate, plus beta times the equity risk premium.

Beta isn't 1 number off a screen. Take your comps' betas. Strip out each company's use. Average the business risk. Re-lever at the structure you're modelling. That's 4 steps, and interviewers ask for all of them.

And use the current yield, not the coupon. A bond issued at 4% that now yields 6.5% costs you 6.5% to refinance. WACC looks forward.

Save this one.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #wacc #valuation

The market already priced it. So why does an acquirer pay 30% above that?

3 reasons, and only 1 of them is synergies.

Control. Buy 2% of a company and you have no say in anything. Buy 51% and you set strategy, appoint the board and direct the cash. A traded share price is what a minority stake costs, and control isn't in it. This is the reason most candidates forget.

Synergies, and say which kind. Cost synergies are overlapping functions and sites. You can count them and they usually land. Revenue synergies are cross-sell and new markets, they're forecast, and they frequently don't arrive. Buyers get discounted accordingly.

Scarcity. Sometimes there's no second asset like it, and that's worth paying for on its own.

Then the question underneath all 3. Who captures the value? If the acquirer pays away 100% of the synergies, the deal is great for the seller and does nothing at all for the buyer.

That's why most large acquisitions disappoint. Closing isn't the test.

Save this.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #mergersandacquisitions #valuation

posts.caption:
A company can post record profit and miss payroll in the same quarter. Here's how.

Revenue is booked when it's earned, not when it's collected. So a business growing 40% a year books profit on cash it hasn't seen yet.

Growth makes it worse, not better.

You buy inventory. You pay staff. You ship. You book the revenue. The customer pays you 60 days later, sometimes 90. Every extra unit of growth widens that gap, and you're the one funding it until it closes.

Then there are 3 more that have nothing to do with working capital. Capex outrunning operating cash. Debt coming due. A one-off legal or restructuring payment that lands in 1 quarter.

Here's the part almost everyone misses, and it's the part they're really asking about.

Where would you look?

The income statement is the last place this shows up. Operating cash flow falling while net income rises is the signal. Receivables up 50% on a 20% revenue increase is the cause.

So name the mechanism, name the line, name the statement. 3 sentences and you're done.

"Bad management" names nothing, and they move on.

Save this for the night before.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #financialmodeling

posts.caption:
"Goodwill is the premium paid." That's the most commonly half-right answer in accounting, and half-right loses the question.

It's purchase price less the fair value of net identifiable assets acquired. Not book value. Fair value.

Here's why that distinction matters. Book value of net assets is 600. On acquisition, property and brands get written up and customer relationships get recognised for the first time, taking you to 750. You paid 1,000. Goodwill is 250, not 400.

The step-up happens first. The residual is what's left.

It's tested, never amortised. Finite-life intangibles get amortised. Goodwill sits on the balance sheet indefinitely and gets tested for impairment at least once a year. Amortising it over 10 years was the old rule and it hasn't applied for 2 decades.

And when it's written down, nothing leaves the building. The charge hits the income statement and equity. It's added straight back on the cash flow statement. Cash is untouched.

What it really is: the buyer admitting in public that it overpaid.

Save this one.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #mergersandacquisitions

posts.caption:
Most people say an LBO is buying a company with debt, then stop talking. That's the setup, not the answer.

5 steps. Sources and uses at entry. Project free cash flow. Sweep that cash against the debt. Exit on EBITDA times a multiple, usually after 5 years. Divide exit equity by entry equity.

So why use debt?

Take a 1,000 purchase funded 60% debt and 40% equity. Your cheque is 400, not 1,000. The same gain in enterprise value now lands on a much thinner slice, so a deal that would have returned 2.0x returns closer to 3.0x. Interest is deductible. And a repayment schedule keeps management honest.

Say the other half too. Use multiplies your losses on exactly the same maths, and if you don't volunteer that, they'll ask.

Returns come from 3 places and they aren't equally reliable. Debt paydown and EBITDA growth are things a sponsor can influence. Multiple expansion is a market call. Build on the first 2 and assume you exit at the same 10x you paid.

Good target? Steady cash flow, low existing debt, low capex. Not a software company growing 80% a year. It burns cash and it can't carry the debt.

Then finish with the number. Exit enterprise value, minus net debt, over your 400.

Save this one.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #privateequity #lbo

posts.caption:
An increase in net working capital is a use of cash. Get that sign backwards and every forecast you build for the rest of your career is wrong in the same direction.

In: receivables, inventory, prepaid expenses, payables, accrued expenses.

Out: cash and short-term debt. Those are financing.

So the textbook version, current assets minus current liabilities, is the wrong number, because it quietly includes both of the things you were supposed to strip out.

Here's the mechanic. Receivables up 50, inventory up 30. That's 80 of cash sitting somewhere other than your bank account. Payables up 20 hands you 20 back, an interest-free loan from your suppliers. Net change: 60 used.

That's it. That's the whole thing.

The cycle in days is DSO plus DIO minus DPO. Days to collect, plus days of inventory, minus the days you take to pay, which is how long your cash is tied up before it comes home.

Some businesses run it negative. A supermarket collects at the till and pays suppliers in 45 days, so growth throws off cash instead of eating it.

Drop the term from your DCF because it looks small in year 1 and you've valued a company that never funds its own growth.

Save this.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #financialmodeling #accounting

posts.caption:
"Cash flow" means 4 different things. Each takes its own discount rate. Mix 2 of them up and your valuation is wrong by a mile.

Unlevered free cash flow. Start with EBIT of 200. Tax it at 25%, so 150. Add D&A of 40, subtract capex of 50, subtract a 10 build in working capital. That's 130, and it sits before interest, so it belongs to lenders and shareholders together. Discount at WACC. You get enterprise value.

Levered free cash flow. Start at net income instead, so after the 30 of interest. Same adjustments, then subtract mandatory repayment. That's what's left for shareholders. Discount at cost of equity. You get equity value, and there's no bridge to build.

Operating cash flow minus capex. The quick one, straight off the statement. It's levered, because operating cash flow already sits after interest paid. People feed this into a WACC-discounted DCF every single day and never notice.

Then EBITDA, which isn't cash flow at all.

It ignores capex. It ignores working capital. It ignores cash taxes and interest. That's 4 omissions, and if you call it a cash proxy you'd better be able to name all 4.

1 rule covers the whole thing. Match the claim to the rate.

Save this before your next model test.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #financialmodeling #valuation

posts.caption:
Why is there no P/EBITDA? 1 rule answers that, and every other multiple question you'll get.

The numerator and the denominator have to belong to the same people.

Enterprise value is the whole business, so it pairs with anything measured before lenders are paid. That's 4 of them: EV/Revenue, EV/EBITDA, EV/EBIT, and EV over unlevered free cash flow.

Equity value is the shareholders' slice, so it pairs with what's left after lenders. That's 3: P/E, price to book, and price over levered free cash flow.

P/EBITDA mixes them. Price is after debt. EBITDA is before it. The ratio describes nobody.

Here's why EV/EBITDA does the heavy lifting. Take 2 identical businesses. Company A has no debt and trades at a P/E of 20. Company B is heavily levered and trades at 12. Same operations, same 100 of EBITDA, and you'd conclude B is 40% cheaper. Their EV/EBITDA is identical, because enterprise value and EBITDA both sit above the capital structure.

Then say what EBITDA hides. Capex, working capital and cash taxes, all 3 ignored. For a capital-intensive business, EV/EBIT is often fairer.

Save this before your next technical.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #financialmodeling

posts.caption:
"Which method gives the highest valuation?" There's a usual order, and the reason matters far more than the order does.

Precedents usually print highest. Comps sit below. The DCF ranges widest of the 4. An LBO sets the floor.

Why precedents beat comps.

A comp is what 1 share trades at, a minority stake with no say in anything. A precedent is what somebody actually paid to own all 100% of it and run it. That price carries a control premium, often 20 to 30%, plus whatever synergies the buyer talked themselves into.

Why the DCF ranges widest. WACC, terminal growth and your year 5 margin are 3 numbers nobody can verify, and a 1% move in any of them swings the answer more than a revenue assumption you'd argue about for a week.

Why the LBO is the floor. A sponsor needs its target return, so there's a hard ceiling on what it can pay. A strategic buyer with synergies goes higher.

Then say which one you'd lean on. Liquid comps, lean on comps. Live sale process, lean on precedents. Stable forecastable business, the DCF earns its place.

Say typically. Then say why.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #mergersandacquisitions

posts.caption:
Somebody gave you 15 minutes. Most people waste 11 of them talking about themselves.

The first 60 seconds: thank them, name whoever connected you, 2 lines on you, and 1 on why you asked for this call specifically. Then stop talking.

Ask what only they can answer. "What's banking like" is a brochure question and you'll get a brochure answer. "How did you end up in this group" and "what surprised you in year 1" are questions nobody else can answer for them.

Show the reading without performing it. 1 specific reference, not 3. "I saw you worked on that deal, what was hard about it?" One is interest. Three is research, and it reads differently.

Minute 13 is the entire call. 2 questions: is there anyone else in the group worth speaking to, and is there anything I should be doing now. Both are easy to say yes to, and 1 of them hands you the next conversation.

Then follow up inside 24 hours, referencing something specific they said so it's obviously not a template.

Save this before your next one.

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #networking #financecareers
posts.first_comment: What's the best question anyone has asked you on a networking call?

posts.caption:
Depreciation goes up by $10. You'll probably get the income statement right, and then lose it on cash.

Pre-tax income drops $10. At a 25% tax rate you pay $2.50 less tax, so net income falls $7.50, not $10.

On the cash flow statement you start from that -7.5 and add the 10 back, because depreciation is an accounting charge and not a single dollar of it actually left the bank. Cash ends up $2.50 higher.

That's the tax you saved.

Balance sheet: PP&E down 10, cash up 2.5, assets down 7.5. Retained earnings down 7.5. It balances.

If yours doesn't, check the tax line first.

Save this for your next technical round.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #threestatements

Equity value to enterprise value. 4 adjustments, and you'll be asked why for each one.

EV is what the operations are worth to everyone who funds them, not just shareholders, so you add debt, preferred stock and minority interest, then take away cash.

Why subtract cash? Whoever buys the company gets it back.

Why add minority interest? If you own 80% of a subsidiary you still consolidate 100% of its EBITDA, so you add the 20% you don't own or your EV/EBITDA comes out too low.

Easy follow-up.

If the company issues $100 of new shares, EV doesn't move. Equity value and cash both rise by 100 and cancel.

Save it before your valuation questions.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #enterprisevalue

"Why investment banking?" Try this test on your answer: would it work just as well for consulting?

"A steep learning curve" fits consulting. "Smart people" fits law. "Passion for finance" fits nothing in particular. None of it's wrong. It just doesn't answer the question.

Build it in 3 beats instead. 1 moment that pulled you toward deals. 1 thing you actually did about it. Then why the analyst job itself is the next step, the modelling, the live transactions, seeing a deal from pitch to close.

Leave exit options out. They hear "I want to leave in 2 years."

Then say it out loud with a timer running. Under 60 seconds.

Which line in your current answer would fail the test?

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #superday #financecareers

All-stock deal. Is it accretive? You can answer in 1 line if you compare the right 2 numbers.

Buyer trades at 20 times earnings and pays 15 times for the target, premium included, which means it's swapping expensive paper for cheaper earnings, so EPS goes up.

Flip them. Dilutive.

Cash deal? You compare the after-tax cost of that cash or debt with the target's earnings yield at the price paid. Yield is 1 over the P/E, so at 20 times it's 5%.

Then add the line I'd want to hear: accretive doesn't mean good. Overpay and EPS can still rise while value falls.

Save this one for M&A questions.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #mergersandacquisitions #accretiondilution

A deferred tax liability is tax you've postponed. Not tax you've avoided.

Companies keep 2 sets of books and both are legal: GAAP for shareholders, tax rules for the tax authority, and depreciation is often faster on the tax side.

Say book depreciation is 10 and tax depreciation is 30. Taxable income is 20 lower, so at 25% you pay 5 less tax than your income statement shows.

That 5 is owed later. So it's a liability.

Later the accelerated depreciation runs out, cash tax climbs above book tax, and the DTL unwinds to 0.

On the cash flow statement, an increase in the DTL gets added back in operating cash flow. You recorded the expense but didn't pay it.

Save it for the accounting round.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #deferredtax

Debt is cheaper than equity. So why doesn't every company borrow as much as it can?

Comment your answer first.

Debt is cheaper for 2 reasons: lenders get paid before shareholders, and interest is tax deductible. At a 25% tax rate, 100 of interest only costs you 75.

But every extra turn of debt puts more fixed claims ahead of equity, so shareholders' returns swing harder and they'll want more for holding the stock. Push further and default gets likelier, so lenders charge you more too.

And the shield? Worth 0 in a year with no profit.

Put it together and WACC falls, bottoms out, then climbs. A U. Your target structure sits near the bottom.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #wacc #corporatefinance

In a DCF, the terminal value is usually the biggest single number. Interviewers know it, so they'll push on it.

Perpetuity growth: final-year FCF times (1 + g), over WACC minus g. Keep g below long-run economic growth, or you've built a company that eventually becomes bigger than the economy.

Exit multiple: year 5 EBITDA times a multiple from today's comps.

Then use each to check the other.

Your growth rate implies a multiple, and your multiple implies a growth rate, so if 1 of them looks absurd you know which assumption to fix.

Last step, and people forget it: TV sits at the end of year 5, so you discount it 5 years.

Save this for DCF questions.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #dcf #valuation

"Where does your beta come from?" It's 4 steps, and you'll be asked for all of them.

Pull the levered betas for your comps.

Each one mixes business risk with that company's own debt, so you unlever them: levered beta over 1 + (1 - tax rate) x D/E. A beta of 1.2 with D/E of 0.5 and a 25% tax rate gives 1.2 / 1.375, about 0.87. Use market values for D/E, not book.

Take the median.

Relever it at the target's own structure. At a D/E of 0.3, 0.87 becomes about 1.07, and that's the number that goes into CAPM.

Save this with your WACC notes.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #wacc #beta

"Any questions for me?" Not the end of the interview. The last part of it.

Ask about their work. "Which deal taught you the most?" gets a real answer.

"What's a typical day like?" gets you the website.

Then ask what the group rewards, something like "what separates analysts who do well here?", because it tells you how they actually judge people and it shows them you're already thinking about being good at the job rather than just getting the offer.

Close the loop. "Is there anything in my background I can clarify?" is your 1 last shot at fixing a weak answer.

Prepare 4. Ask 2. Skip pay and hours.

What's the best question you've asked?

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #interviewtips #superday

Why does every banker quote EBITDA? And what can't it see?

It's before interest, so you can compare 2 companies with very different debt loads, which is why it pairs with enterprise value and never with equity value.

It's before D&A too.

The blind spot is capex. Company A and Company B both have EBITDA of 100. A spends 10 on capex, B spends 60, so after that you're looking at 90 against 40.

It misses working capital and tax as well. A fast-growing business can post rising EBITDA while its cash disappears into receivables.

A comparison tool, not cash flow. Say both halves.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #ebitda #valuation

Prices are rising. LIFO or FIFO? Work it with 3 numbers.

You bought 1 unit at 10, then another at 14, and sold 1 for 20.

FIFO expenses the oldest cost: COGS 10, gross profit 10, tax at 25% is 2.5.
LIFO expenses the newest: COGS 14, gross profit 6, tax 1.5.

So LIFO shows less profit but keeps more cash, because it pays less tax.

FIFO wins on the balance sheet. Inventory sits at 14, closer to what it'd cost to replace. LIFO leaves it at 10.

Last point: IFRS doesn't allow LIFO. US GAAP does. Compare across the two and you adjust first.

Save it for the accounting round.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #inventory

"Why our bank?" Run the swap test. Put a different bank's name in your answer. If it still works, rewrite it.

"A leading global franchise" passes for every bank on your list. That's the problem.

Name the group you'd join and what it actually covers.

Use 1 real conversation: who you spoke to, what they told you, why it stuck. It beats a paragraph of research.

Mention 1 deal the group worked on and why it interested you. 1, explained, not a list copied off their site.

Finish on fit. How the team works and why that matches what you've already done.

Does your answer pass?

#investmentbanking #ibrecruiting #networking #superday

2 times your money in 5 years. What's the IRR? You should know it without a calculator.

MOIC is exit equity over entry equity. Put in 100, get 200, that's 2 times. It says nothing about time.

IRR does. 2 times in 3 years is about 26% a year. The same 2 times over 5 years is about 15%.

The 3 to memorise:
2 times, 5 years: about 15%
3 times, 5 years: about 25%
2 times, 3 years: about 26%

And don't divide. 100% over 5 years isn't 20% a year, because returns compound.

Funds report both numbers, because a quick flip can post a big IRR on a small gain.

#investmentbanking #privateequity #lbo #ibinterview

A company pays a $10 dividend. The trick is the statement where nothing happens.

Income statement: no change. You're distributing profit after it's earned, not paying an expense.

Cash flow statement: 10 out, in financing, next to buybacks and debt repaid.

Balance sheet: cash down 10, retained earnings down 10.

Then the follow-up they love, which is what happens to enterprise value, and the answer is nothing, because equity value falls by about 10 as the cash goes to shareholders and cash falls by the same 10.

The operations didn't change. Neither did EV.

Save it next to your depreciation walk-through.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #threestatements

$100 of revenue at a software company, or $100 at a grocer. Which would you pay more for?

Drop your pick in the comments first.

Revenue isn't profit. Grocers run on thin margins and software on high ones, so the same 100 of sales turns into very different cash for you as the buyer.

Growth moves the multiple. You're paying today for cash that arrives in year 3, 5, 10.

Durability too.

Subscription revenue that renews is far easier to forecast than sales you have to win again every year.

So I'd usually take software. But a slow, loss-making software company can be worth less than a steady grocer, so say "it depends", then say on what.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #valuation #multiples

How do leases change EBITDA? It depends on where the company reports, and that's the whole point of the question.

Since 2019 for listed companies, IFRS 16 and US GAAP's ASC 842 both put most leases on the balance sheet: a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.

Under IFRS 16, rent leaves operating costs and comes back as depreciation and interest. Both sit below EBITDA, so EBITDA goes up.

Under US GAAP, an operating lease keeps 1 straight-line cost inside operating expenses. EBITDA doesn't move.

So before you compare a European comp with a US one, check. If lease costs sit below EBITDA, lease liabilities belong in EV.

#investmentbanking #ibinterview #accounting #ifrs16

Cost synergies or revenue synergies? Buyers trust 1 of them a lot more.

Cost synergies are what you can cut: a duplicate head office, 2 IT systems running side by side, 2 purchasing teams. Once the deal closes, they're in management's hands.

Revenue synergies are what you hope to sell.

Cross-selling, new markets, bigger contracts. They depend on customers doing something they haven't done yet, which is why boards and lenders lean on cost synergies when they justify a premium.

Neither shows up on day 1. You pay integration costs first, then synergies phase in, part in year 1 and more in year 2, before you hit a full run-rate.

Count what you control.

"Tell me about a time you failed." They're not grading the failure. They're grading what came after it.

"I work too hard" is the real failure here. It tells them you won't own a mistake on a live deal.

Pick something that mattered, that was at least partly your fault, and that didn't end anything.

Own your part in 1 plain sentence. I, not we.

Spend most of the answer on the fix: what you did, and the habit you kept.

Then show it stuck. 1 later moment where you did it right is worth more than "I learned a lot".

Why does an LBO model have a circular reference? Because the business really works that way.

Interest depends on debt, debt paydown depends on cash, and cash depends on net income, which depends on interest. Calculate interest on the average balance and you're right back where you started.

3 fixes.

1. Turn on iterative calculation in Excel.
2. Add a circuit breaker, a switch that sets interest to 0, so 1 error can't spread through your model.
3. Use the opening debt balance. No loop, but you lose a bit of precision when debt's paid down fast.

Name the loop. Give a fix. Say what it costs you.

Is stock-based compensation a real expense? "It's non-cash" is only half the answer.

It hits the income statement, but no cash leaves, so you add it back in operating cash flow.

The cost shows up somewhere else. Say you own 1% of a company with 100 million shares. It issues 2 million to staff, and your 1 million shares are now about 0.98% of it.

That's the cost. Dilution.

In valuation, count it once: either treat it as a cash cost and cut free cash flow, or keep it added back and put the future dilution in your diluted share count.

Doing neither is the mistake I'd look for.

Save this before a tech or growth company interview.

The mid-year convention looks like a minor DCF switch. The follow-up question is where people trip.

Cash doesn't all arrive on 31 December. It comes in through the year, so each year's cash flow is discounted from the middle: 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 and so on. Less discounting, so the value goes up.

The follow-up: what about terminal value?

Perpetuity growth TV extends those same mid-year cash flows, so it's discounted at n - 0.5.

Exit multiple TV doesn't move. A multiple prices the business at 1 point in time, the end of the forecast, so it stays at year n.

Save it with your DCF notes.
